newsitem.title: USA: Clinton meets legislators on campaign finance reform.
newsitem.headline: Clinton meets legislators on campaign finance reform.

text.p: President Bill Clinton met the sponsors of a campaign finance reform bill on Thursday, with the legislators saying afterwards it would be difficult to overhaul the system but that the chances have now improved.

Under fire for his Democratic party's fund-raising tactics during last year's election, Clinton has repeatedly called in recent months for revamping the system under which hundreds of millions of dollars flow to both parties.

The president, whose party returned more than $1.5 million in questionable contributions during the campaign, on Tuesday challenged Republicans to agree to a ban on large donations and accused them of accepting questionable contributions as well.
To draw attention to the issue, Clinton invited the four sponsors of the McCain-Feingold bill that would tighten the rules for raising political funds to the White House.

Those at the meeting included its four sponsors: Arizona Republican Sen. John McCain, Wisconsin Democratic Sen. Russell Feingold, Republican Representative Christopher Shays of Connecticut and Democratic Representative Martin Meehan of Massachussetts.
Anne McBride, president of the Common Cause lobby group that has long sought compaign finance reform, also attended and was effusive in her praise of the legislators afterwards.

"I think that we have got the best chance in 20 years to enact real reform," McBride told reporters after the 45-minute meeting. "What is a terrible, terrible, rotten, corrupt system can be changed, but it takes the kind of courageous and strong leadership willing to set aside partisan differences."

While all four sponsors of the bill made upbeat statements about the chances of passing campaign finance reform, they did not minimise the difficulties of persuading legislators to vote to change a system under which they were all elected.
"I'm not saying that we will do it but I'm saying that the chances of meaningful reform ... are better than they've been since 1973," McCain told reporters after the meeting.

White House spokesman Barry Toiv said Clinton and Vice President Al Gore had promised the legislators they would do whatever they could to help pass the legislation, which would set voluntary limits on campaign spending and require most funds come from a congressional candidate's home state.
"The president and vice president made it clear that we need to do this in a bipartisan way," Toiv added. "That it is not going to get done if it is viewed as one party taking on another party."
